:::{#thm-invertible-rank}
#### A square matrix is invertible exactly when it has full column rank

An $n \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$ is invertible (@def-invertible-matrix)
exactly when $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = n$
(full column rank, @def-full-column-rank),
that is, exactly when $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A}) = \cb{\vzero_n}$.

:::

::: proof

**Invertible implies rank $n$.**
If $\matr{A} \vecf{x} = \vzero_n$, then

$$
\ba
\vecf{x}
&= \matr{I}_n \vecf{x}
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\\
&= (\matr{A}^{-1} \matr{A})\,\vecf{x}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{A}^{-1}\,(\matr{A} \vecf{x})
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{A}^{-1}\,\vzero_n
&& \text{(} \matr{A} \vecf{x} = \vzero_n \text{)}
\\
&= \vzero_n,
&& \text{(@def-matvec-mult)}
\ea
$$

so $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A}) = \cb{\vzero_n}$, the nullity is $0$,
and $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = n$ (@thm-rank-nullity).

**Rank $n$ implies invertible.**
Every system $\matr{A} \vecf{y} = \vecf{b}$ has exactly one solution
(@cor-solution-unique, both parts, with $m = n$).
Let $\vecf{y}_j$ solve $\matr{A} \vecf{y}_j = \vecf{e}_j$ (@def-indicator-vector),
and let $\matr{B}$ have columns $\vecf{y}_1, \ldots, \vecf{y}_n$.
Column $j$ of $\matr{A} \matr{B}$ is $\matr{A} \vecf{y}_j = \vecf{e}_j$ (@def-matrix-mult),
so $\matr{A} \matr{B} = \matr{I}_n$.
For the other order,

$$
\ba
\matr{A}\,(\matr{B} \matr{A} - \matr{I}_n)
&= \matr{A} \matr{B} \matr{A} - \matr{A} \matr{I}_n
&& \text{(@thm-scalar-matmul, @thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_n \matr{A} - \matr{A} \matr{I}_n
&& \text{(} \matr{A} \matr{B} = \matr{I}_n \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{A} - \matr{A}
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\\
&= \matr{0}_{n \times n},
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

so every column of $\matr{B} \matr{A} - \matr{I}_n$ is in $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A}) = \cb{\vzero_n}$
(@def-matrix-mult),
and $\matr{B} \matr{A} = \matr{I}_n$.
So $\matr{B}$ satisfies @def-invertible-matrix.
The two conditions in the statement are equivalent by @thm-rank-nullity:
the nullity is $0$ exactly when $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A}) = \cb{\vzero_n}$,
because a subspace of dimension $0$ has the empty list as a basis, whose span is $\cb{\vzero}$
(@def-dimension, @def-span), and $\cb{\vzero}$ has dimension $0$ (@exm-dimension).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-invertible-rank}
#### Rank decides invertibility

- $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ of @exm-invertible-matrix has rank $2$:
  $c_1 (2, 0) + c_2 (1, 1) = (2c_1 + c_2, c_2)$ is $\vzero$ only if $c_2 = 0$ and then $c_1 = 0$.
  So it is invertible, as that example found by exhibiting the inverse.
- $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ has rank less than $2$:
  $(1, -1)$ is a nonzero vector in its null space.
  So it is singular, as @exm-invertible-matrix found.

:::
